A detailed examination of the situation in Assam reveals that if the methods used to determine eligibility for mass drug administration fail to consider high-risk groups within the population, the intervention will not succeed in eradicating the disease and will neglect those who are most in need of treatment. 2. To combat the spread of lymphatic filariasis, mass drug administration of preventive chemotherapy is implemented in endemic areas of India. 3. Districts are deemed eligible for mass drug administration when the reported microfilaria rate exceeds 1%, as determined through sampling. 4. Tea garden workers account for 39% of cases, and their microfilaria rate is significantly higher than the rest of the population, whether urban or rural, which is less than 1% when tea garden workers are excluded. 5. Despite being a high-risk group, the eligibility of tea garden workers for the intervention depends on the microfilaria rate in their district of residence. 6. Consequently, tea garden workers in districts where their numbers are insufficient to raise the district-wide microfilaria rate above 1% will not benefit from mass drug administration. This is a common issue in Assam, as tea garden workers are dispersed across the state rather than concentrated in specific areas. 7. This example underscores that population-level thresholds for mass drug administration may fail to account for subpopulations with higher infection prevalence. 8. In such cases, public health agencies should weigh the expected benefits, risks, and burdens of whole-population mass drug administration against more targeted interventions for these subpopulations. 9. Governments and donors have an obligation to ensure the quality of vaccines and drugs used in vaccine campaigns and mass drug administration programs. 10. Government officials are responsible for promoting the health and well-being of their citizens. Therefore, those managing vaccine campaigns or mass drug administration programs, as well as supporting donors, must have confidence in the quality of the vaccines and drugs being used. 11. This requires careful procurement practices to avoid counterfeit or substandard products and oversight of all aspects of storage, transportation, and distribution. 12. The CYD-TDV dengue vaccine became controversial because it benefits seropositive individuals (those previously infected with dengue) but increases the risk for seronegative individuals (those never infected). 13. The suspected reason for worse outcomes in seronegative individuals is that the vaccine acts like an asymptomatic first dengue infection, priming them for a more severe second infection. 14. Without pre-vaccination screening to exclude seronegative individuals, the public health gains from dengue vaccination come at the cost of exposing seronegative individuals to greater risk. 15. This issue is further complicated by the lack of rapid diagnostic tools to determine serostatus, logistical challenges, and the potential for false positives in screening. 16. The use of the CYD-TDV vaccine raises ethical dilemmas, such as whether it is acceptable to maximize overall welfare while knowingly exposing some individuals to risk. 17. In populations with high prevalence rates, mass vaccination without screening may benefit seropositive individuals and provide overall population-level benefits but would harm some seronegative individuals. 18. If seronegative individuals could be identified and excluded, harm to them could be prevented, making the failure to screen ethically problematic. 19. However, if screening is not technically feasible, some argue that failing to vaccinate would lead to preventable harm to seropositive individuals who would benefit from vaccination. 20. The public may not tolerate measures that increase the risk of severe illness for some, especially when vaccination programs target children, who are often considered a vulnerable group and more likely to be seronegative. 21. The peculiarities of the dengue vaccine, such as variable risk-benefit ratios and the need for pre-vaccination screening, pose communication challenges that may erode public trust in other vaccination programs. 22. In 2017, when evidence clarified the risk of severe dengue among vaccinated seronegative individuals, the vaccine was already privately available in several countries, and public immunization programs were underway in parts of Brazil and the Philippines. 23. This controversy damaged public trust in immunization in those countries, leading to increased vaccine refusal. 24. Public health surveillance is defined as the continuous, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health-related data needed for planning, implementing, and evaluating public health practices. 25. Countries have an ethical duty to engage in public health surveillance because, without it, population health cannot be protected, and inequalities cannot be adequately addressed. 26. Once surveillance data are collected, countries have a moral duty to use the data actively to promote better health outcomes. 27. This includes the obligation to share surveillance data with relevant public health officials and others involved in disease prevention and control efforts, while protecting individual confidentiality. 28. Surveillance of both vectors and vector-borne diseases is crucial because many infected individuals are asymptomatic or have mild symptoms that go unreported. 29. Early identification of disease outbreaks requires ongoing collection, analysis, and interpretation of data on infection prevalence, vector movement, and environmental risk factors. 30. Vector surveillance is one of the four foundations of the World Health Assembly-approved Global Vector Control Response Strategy for 2017–2030. 31. Screening is defined as the presumptive identification of unrecognized disease in an apparently healthy, asymptomatic population through tests, examinations, or other procedures that can be applied rapidly and easily. 32. Screening is sometimes used as part of surveillance, such as testing a population for a vector-borne disease during an outbreak response. 33. Screening can also be used for non-surveillance purposes, such as offering screening for vector-borne diseases to at-risk individuals to promote early access to care. 34. Surveillance of private living spaces to identify vector sources is an important component of vector control programs. 35. Public health workers should seek the consent of property owners or occupants before inspecting private living spaces for potential vector sources. 36. If the owner or occupant is absent or unwilling to allow the inspection, a judicial warrant or similar authorization should be obtained, except in emergency situations. 37. Such authorization should only be granted if there is a genuine public health need for the inspection that outweighs the burdens on the owner or occupant. 38. The ethical obligation to obtain consent or external authorization applies equally to aerial inspections by drones. 39. Countries should assess their laws and policies related to surveillance of private living spaces to ensure they conform to ethical principles. 40. Individually identifiable surveillance data should not be shared with law enforcement agencies without express legal authorization, which should only be granted in compelling circumstances. 41. Inappropriate sharing of surveillance data with law enforcement threatens public trust in public health surveillance, creating a disincentive for individuals to seek healthcare or report information honestly. 42. The use of drone technology for disease surveillance has grown, particularly in controlling arboviral diseases such as dengue, Zika virus, chikungunya, and yellow fever. 43. Drones are used to identify standing water in structures and containers beyond the visual acuity of inspectors. 44. In Singapore, the National Environment Agency uses drones to facilitate inspections of hard-to-reach areas as part of its vector control strategy. 45. Public health inspectors licensed by the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore are the only individuals allowed to pilot drones for regulatory inspection work.
